content: Mastitis is defined as inflammation of the breast tissue. It most commonly affects breastfeeding mothers, a condition referred to as puerperal mastitis. Non-puerperal mastitis, on the other hand, occurs in individuals who are not breastfeeding. While rare, mastitis can also occur in men. It is important to differentiate mastitis from inflammatory breast cancer, as the symptoms of both conditions can be very similar. A thorough medical history and appropriate diagnostic investigations are necessary to rule out malignancy. The terminology and classification of mastitis can vary geographically, with some regions using the term to describe both puerperal and non-puerperal cases. Chronic cystic mastitis, also known as fibrocystic disease, is characterized by non-cancerous lumps in the breast. Historically, mastitis was first described by Dr. G. Ranney of Michigan and later documented in 1887 by Dr. Charles J. Wright in the British Medical Journal. Between the 1930s and 1960s, an epidemic form of puerperal mastitis was frequently observed in hospital nurseries in industrialized countries. This was during a time when hospital deliveries became more common, breastfeeding was not widely promoted, and antibiotics were just beginning to be used. Staphylococcal infections, particularly penicillin-resistant strains of Staphylococcus aureus, were identified as the primary cause of these outbreaks, with transmission occurring between nursery personnel, infants, and mothers. Epidemic mastitis was thus regarded as a hospital-acquired disease. Mastitis can be classified into subtypes based on etiology, duration, anatomical location, immunological association, and patient age. Examples include granulomatous mastitis, lupus mastitis, and pre-pubertal mastitis. The pathophysiology of non-puerperal mastitis often begins with inflammation of the ductal and lobular systems, potentially involving surrounding tissues. This condition is typically caused by secretory stasis. In contrast, puerperal mastitis occurs when bacteria, often from the patient’s skin or the infant’s mouth or nostrils, enter a milk duct through a crack in the nipple. The primary causative agents of mastitis are bacteria, most commonly Staphylococcus aureus, Staphylococcus epidermidis, Streptococcus, E. coli, and Mycoplasma. Fungal infections, particularly Candida species, can also cause mastitis, especially when transmitted from the infant’s oral cavity. Mastitis must be differentiated from other conditions that cause breast pain or swelling, such as galactocele, breast engorgement, mastodynia, fibrocystic breast disease, breast cancer, fibroadenoma, Mondor’s disease, and breast trauma. Globally, the prevalence of mastitis ranges from 1,000 to 10,000 cases per 100,000 individuals, with an average prevalence of 4,700 per 100,000. The incidence of puerperal mastitis ranges from 2,900 to 9,500 cases per 100,000 deliveries, with an average of 6,200 cases per 100,000 deliveries within the first seven weeks postpartum. Approximately 3% to 11% of individuals with mastitis may develop a breast abscess. Breastfeeding mothers aged 21 to 35 years are most commonly affected, with the highest occurrence in those aged 30 to 34 years. There is no significant racial predisposition to mastitis, but the incidence is higher in developing countries. Risk factors for mastitis include breastfeeding, particularly in women with sore or cracked nipples or a history of mastitis. Other risk factors include using a single breastfeeding position, wearing tight-fitting bras, and having conditions such as diabetes, chronic illness, AIDS, or an impaired immune system. Non-breastfeeding-related mastitis may, in rare cases, indicate a form of breast cancer. The World Health Organization states that there is no specific screening modality available for mastitis. If left untreated, up to 11% of patients with puerperal mastitis may develop a breast abscess. Complications include recurrence, milk stasis, and abscess formation. The prognosis is generally favorable, with mastitis resolving quickly with appropriate antibiotic therapy. However, smokers, particularly those with non-puerperal mastitis, have a worse prognosis and a higher recurrence rate of breast abscesses. The diagnosis of mastitis is primarily clinical. Patients often present a few days postpartum with localized breast complaints. The affected area is typically near the nipple and areola, most commonly on the upper inner side of the breast. Mastitis usually affects only one breast, and it is rare for the entire breast to be involved. Common symptoms include redness, localized pain, and warmth in the affected area. Some patients may also experience flu-like symptoms, such as aches, shivering, and chills, though these are less common. Physical examination findings may include lowto high-grade fever, breast tenderness, and swelling. Laboratory findings may show a positive bacterial culture of breast milk in some cases, though this is not routinely performed due to the potential for false positives or negatives. Cultures are recommended in severe, unusual, or hospital-acquired infections or when there is no response to antibiotics after two days. A complete blood count may reveal elevated neutrophils, though this is non-specific. There are no characteristic ECG findings for mastitis, but it has been reported to unmask Type 1 Brugada Syndrome, with ECG abnormalities resolving once mastitis is treated. Imaging modalities such as X-rays and CT scans are not diagnostic for mastitis. However, MRI is the most specific imaging tool for diagnosing mastitis, particularly non-puerperal cases. On contrast-enhanced MRI, non-puerperal mastitis often appears as non-mass-like lesions with heterogeneous signal intensity. Ultrasound may show edema of fatty tissue, hypoechoic areas, dilated ducts, fluid collections, or irregular hypoechoic masses. Treatment for puerperal mastitis primarily involves supportive care, including massage, heat application, cold compresses, and frequent breastfeeding. Non-puerperal mastitis treatment depends on the underlying condition and may include prolactin-inhibiting agents, antimicrobial therapy, and NSAIDs. Granulomatous mastitis has been treated with a combination of steroids and prolactin-inhibiting medications. Surgical intervention is generally reserved for complicated cases, such as abscess formation requiring drainage or granulomatous mastitis requiring excision. Preventive measures include avoiding risk factors and adhering to best practices for breastfeeding. These include early initiation of breastfeeding, proper breastfeeding techniques, unrestricted and exclusive breastfeeding, and skilled support for mothers, especially during the early postpartum period.
